title: Soils
text:
Five prepared datasets hold 20,690 located profiles. They differ in where they sample, how deep they go and which variables they carry, and that shapes every comparison that follows.







These counts are not independent. WoSIS, the National Pedon Database and the peat compilations share profiles. Layers within a core are repeated depth observations, not separate locations. Profiles have not been deduplicated across datasets here.

NCSCDv2 is exactly zero at 2.1% of points, mostly in the Pacific Maritime and Arctic Cordillera (rock and ice map units). These are recorded values and are kept; leaving them out gives r = -0.03, so the weak relationship is not caused by zeros. NCSCDv2 assigns stocks to soil-map polygons, while SoilGrids predicts each pixel, which is one reason their patterns differ.

Across the shared area the median Sothe:NCSCDv2 ratio is 2.7 (interquartile range 1.4–5.3, points where NCSCDv2 is above zero). A ratio near 1 everywhere would support reading Sothe as 0–1 m kg C/m²; a consistently large ratio would point to a units or depth difference. The two maps also use different methods (pixel prediction versus soil-map polygons), so part of the gap is genuine disagreement. The profile comparison below adds field evidence.




Both model the full peat column, so peat thickness and whole-column carbon can be compared directly. Li (30 m) is averaged to the PEATGRIDS 1 km grid.

Within each product, Li’s whole-column carbon follows Li’s peat depth almost exactly (r = 1.00 across sampled pixels), whereas PEATGRIDS carbon barely follows PEATGRIDS thickness (r = 0.10). The two products build carbon from depth in different ways, so similar thickness does not give similar carbon.

This is a comparison, not a validation: some datasets trained some maps (see above), and a 250 m pixel average is not the same support as a soil core.

These profiles are few and peat-heavy, so this narrows the question but does not settle it.

title: Where Canada’s carbon maps agree, and where they don’t
text:
Read the sections

Forest: forest plot data (placeholder until plots are ingested), the training data and covariates behind each forest map, and SCANFI vs ESA CCI aboveground biomass.
Soils: the five profile datasets compared with each other, the training data and covariates behind each soil map, map-to-map comparisons at matching depths, and maps against profiles.
Methods: the rules, grids, unit conversions, sampling design and limitations.
State of Data summary: the inventory this comparison builds on.

title: Where Canada’s carbon maps agree, and where they don’t
section: What this comparison does not claim
text:
What this comparison does not claim

Agreement between two maps is not accuracy; both can share the same training data or the same blind spots.
Differences are reported on each pair’s coarser native grid; they say nothing about finer detail.
Profile comparisons set a soil core beside a pixel average. Several profile datasets trained some of the maps, so agreement there is not independent validation.
The Sothe 0–100 cm comparison is provisional: its depth is a working assumption and its stored units are unverified.

title: Methods
text:
Question
Where do Canadian carbon products agree or disagree when compared like with like, and how do soil maps compare with field profiles?


Estimand
Per-pixel differences (A − B) on each pair’s coarser native grid, summarised as mean difference, RMSD, Pearson r and share within ±25%, nationally and by terrestrial ecozone. At profiles: map value at the containing pixel vs the thickness-weighted observed value for the same interval.


Data roles
Maps are products being compared; none is treated as truth. Profiles are observations, but not independent validation where they trained a map. Ecozones are reporting units only.


Method
Documented unit conversion, mean aggregation of the finer product to the coarser grid, differencing and descriptive statistics. No modelling, gap-filling or bias correction.


Not part of this analysis
Deriving stocks from concentration × bulk density for maps; deduplicating profiles across datasets; forest plot comparisons (no plots ingested yet); propagating map uncertainty.

title: Methods
text:
Rules for pairing products

Same quantity, same depth or pool. Products are paired only when both report the same quantity (e.g. SOC concentration) for the same depth interval (e.g. 0–5 cm) or the same pool and year. Everything else is listed, with the reason, in the “not compared” tables.
Coarser grid per pair. Each pair is compared on the coarser of its two native grids. The finer product is mean-aggregated (Earth Engine reduceResolution, mean of contributing pixels) to that grid. Nothing is upsampled, because resampling a coarse map to a finer grid adds no information.
Documented units only. Values are converted with the providers’ documented factors to one unit per quantity. No other rescaling.




All pairs. In every pair B is the coarser product, so the comparison grid is B’s native grid.

title: Methods
text:
Sampling design for map statistics
Statistics are computed from 30,000 random points, uniform in area. They are drawn in Canada Albers equal-area (ESRI:102001) within the terrestrial ecozones, seed 42. The peat pairs use 1,500 points in the Hudson Plain ecozone (seed 43). At each point both products are read on the pair’s comparison grid. Points where either product has no data are dropped for that pair. For aboveground biomass, points where both products are zero are also dropped, so shared non-forest does not inflate agreement.
Random sampling keeps the statistics cheap and unbiased by area. The map figures are display summaries: Earth Engine averages each product to the display grid (about 7 km per pixel nationally, 1.5 km in the Hudson Plain) before differencing. They show broad patterns, not pixel-level detail.

title: Methods
text:
Profiles

Depth matching: each profile’s layers are combined into the map intervals by thickness-weighted mean, only where the layers cover the whole interval with no gaps or overlaps. No extrapolation and no splines.
Stocks at 0–30 and 0–100 cm: sums of each dataset’s own layer stock values times the fraction of each layer inside the interval. No bulk density is gap-filled.
Depth datum: each preparation’s own. NPDB organic horizons have negative depths; following the NPDB preparation (datum = profile top), depths are shifted so the profile top is 0.
Map values: each profile takes the value of the map pixel that contains it, at the map’s native grid.
Units: organic carbon in g/kg (WoSIS is stored in g/kg; the other datasets in %, ×10); bulk density in g/cm³; stocks in kg C/m². Riley bulk-density units are unverified.

title: Methods
text:
Ecozones
Canada’s 15 terrestrial ecozones from the AAFC National Ecological Framework (ecozone_shp.zip, Open Government Licence – Canada), stored in Comparison/data/ecozones/. Each sampled point and profile takes the ecozone it falls in.

title: Methods
text:
Limitations

Agreement is not accuracy. Two maps can agree because they share training data or covariates.
Support mismatch. A soil core or inventory plot is a few square metres; the pixels are 30 m to about 1.3 km.
Temporal mismatch. Profiles span 1939–2017; maps represent their own reference periods.
Masks differ. Products exclude water, urban, bedrock or non-forest differently; comparisons use only points where both have data.
Unverified encodings. The Sothe stock’s units and depth, Riley bulk density, and imported encodings of Geng and Li are flagged in the repository QC register.

title: Methods
text:
Reproduce
From Comparison/analysis/ with the project environment (requirements.txt) and Earth Engine access:
Rscript R/01_profile_intervals.R
Rscript R/02_peat_core_depths.R
python gee/01_sample_pairs.py
python gee/02_sample_profiles.py
python gee/03_pair_maps.py
Then from Comparison/, quarto render writes the site to Comparison/_site/, and quarto publish gh-pages publishes it to the repository’s gh-pages branch for GitHub Pages. The site renders from the files in Comparison/data/, so re-rendering does not need Earth Engine.
